segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So be imitators of God, as beloved children,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and walk in love, just as Christ also loved us and gave himself up for us, an offering and sacrifice to God, a fragrant aroma.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But sexual immorality and impurity of any kind, or greed, must not even be named among you, as is proper for holy ones,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: nor obscenity, nor foolish talk or coarse joking, which are out of place, but rather thanksgiving.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For you know this for certain: no one who is sexually immoral or impure or greedy—which is to be an idolater—has any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Let no one deceive you with empty words, for because of these things the wrath of God is coming upon the sons of disobedience.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So do not become their partners;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light—

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for the fruit of the light is found in all goodness and righteousness and truth—

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: testing what is pleasing to the Lord,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and take no part in the fruitless works of darkness, but instead expose them,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for it is shameful even to speak of the things they do in secret.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But all things, when exposed by the light, become visible,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for everything that becomes visible is light. Therefore it says:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Wake up, sleeper, and rise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So watch carefully how you walk, not as unwise people but as wise,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: making the most of the time, because the days are evil.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Therefore do not be foolish, but understand what the Lord’s will is.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And do not get drunk on wine, which leads to reckless living, but be filled by the Spirit,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: speaking to one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making music to the Lord with your heart,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: always giving thanks for everything to God the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: submitting to one another in the fear of Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Wives, submit to your own husbands as to the Lord,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: because a husband is head of his wife as Christ also is head of the assembly—he himself the Savior of the body.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But as the assembly submits to Christ, so also wives should submit to their husbands in everything.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ also loved the assembly and gave himself up for her,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that he might make her holy, cleansing her by the washing of water with the word,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that he himself might present the assembly to himself in splendor, without stain or wrinkle or anything of the kind, but holy and without blemish.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In the same way husbands also ought to love their own wives as their own bodies. He who loves his own wife loves himself,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for no one ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ also does the assembly,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: because we are members of his body.

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be joined to his wife, and the two will become one flesh.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: This hidden meaning is great—but I am speaking about Christ and the assembly.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Still, each one of you also must love his own wife as himself, and the wife is to respect her husband.

notes.note: The traditional “saints” now suggests canonized individuals or people of unusual virtue. The Greek word is used of all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint’s language for Israel. Many translations keep “saints”; others use “God’s people” or “his holy people”.

Some manuscripts read “the fruit of the Spirit”, which is what the King James Version translates. The earliest and best witnesses read “light”, and “Spirit” is generally explained as a copyist’s assimilation to Galatians 5:22.

“By the light” could go either with “exposed” or with “become visible”, and the verb could be passive (“is made visible”) or middle (“becomes visible”). The argument of verses 13–14 is compressed and its exact logic is disputed. The likely point is that what the light exposes is brought into the light and so, like the readers themselves in verse 8, can become light.

The introduction is the formula used for quoting Scripture (as in 4:8), but the lines that follow do not match any known passage of the Old Testament. Most scholars think they come from an early Christian hymn, perhaps one used at baptism, possibly echoing Isaiah 26:19 and 60:1. The source is uncertain.

The Greek is literally “be filled in spirit”. The traditional “filled with the Spirit” treats the Spirit as what fills the believer, as wine fills the drunkard. Greek normally expresses that with a different construction, so many grammarians take the phrase as the means or sphere, “by the Spirit” or “in the Spirit”. A few read it as “in your spirit”.

Most modern versions soften this to “reverence for Christ”. The Greek word is the ordinary one for fear, used here as in the Septuagint’s “fear of the Lord” for awe before one to whom account is owed. The matching verb closes the section in verse 33, where it is rendered “respect”.

The earliest form of the text has no verb in this verse: it reads “wives, to your own husbands as to the Lord”, borrowing “submitting” from verse 21. Many manuscripts supply a form of the verb, in varying positions. The verb is supplied here so the sentence stands in English, but the instruction to wives is grammatically an instance of the mutual submission of verse 21.

The meaning of “head” as a metaphor is disputed. The majority view is that it implies authority or leadership, which fits the talk of submission here and the use in 1:22. Others argue for “source” or “the prominent one”, noting that this passage develops the image as care and self-giving, not command. The literal word is kept so the head-and-body imagery remains visible.

The Greek word meant a gathering of people: a city’s civic assembly, and in the Septuagint Israel assembled before God. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. Here the word refers to the whole community of believers, pictured as Christ’s bride and body.

The Greek verb is built on the ordinary word for “holy”, the same word used of the assembly in verse 27. “Make holy” keeps that link visible. Most traditional versions use “sanctify”; the meaning is not in dispute.

notes.phrase: the washing of water with the word
notes.traditional: the washing of water by the word
notes.note: The washing probably alludes both to a bride’s bath before her wedding and to baptism. “The word” is literally “in a spoken word”, and what it refers to is uncertain: the proclaimed gospel, a confession or formula spoken at baptism, or Christ’s own pledge to his bride. It is also unclear whether the phrase goes with “cleansing” or with “make her holy”.

notes.traditional: members of his body, of his flesh, and of his bones
notes.note: Many later manuscripts add “of his flesh and of his bones”, echoing Genesis 2:23, and the King James Version includes the words. The earliest witnesses lack them, and most editors regard them as an addition. A minority argue they were accidentally omitted.

The Greek word means a secret, especially one that God discloses, and English “mystery” wrongly suggests a puzzle or something beyond understanding. Here it most likely refers to the deeper significance of the “one flesh” saying just quoted, which the writer applies to Christ and the assembly. Most versions keep “mystery”. Some interpreters take the secret to be the union of Christ and the assembly itself, or human marriage.

The verb is literally “fear”, matching “the fear of Christ” in verse 21 and framing the section. In household contexts it denotes deference and regard, not being afraid, and “fear her husband” would mislead a modern reader. Some interpreters prefer to keep “fear” in both verses to show the link.

candidates.reason: The Semitic “walk” for conduct recurs throughout Paul and John, and translations split between “walk” and “live”; one policy is needed.
Recurs across the Gospels, Acts, the letters and Revelation with renderings ranging from “fornication” to “sexual immorality” to “prostitution”; the cognate πόρνος should match.
Used in the household codes, Romans 13 and 1 Peter; “submit”, “be subject” and “be subordinate” carry different tones and should not vary by chapter.
Fear directed at God or Christ (and the verb φοβέομαι in v. 33) is variously rendered “fear”, “reverence”, “respect” and “awe” across the New Testament and needs a consistent rule.
God’s ὀργή recurs in Paul, John and Revelation; “wrath” versus “anger” is a register choice that should be uniform.
